puffin: Cache puff stream in puffpatch Currently without caching the puff stream, the OS updates can be very slow. For example, a back of envelope calculation can show that if we don't cache the puff stream, we may need to read and puff the entire deflate stream (about 500 MB) 160 times which can be very slow. And examination shows that updates can take more than one hour to finish on a veyron_minnie. It may not be reasonable to keep memory usage low but keep the CPU usage high for extended periods of time. The other rationale behind caching the puff stream is that if we only use bsdiff, then we have to keep large patches in memory when applying the patch. But since puffin reduced the patch size by a large factor (so to keep a much smaller patch in memory), then it won't be as bad to cache some memory for faster patching. It is basically a trade-off between CPU time and memory. We may end up using the same amount of memory (which in practice is not going to happen, we will use much less), but the payload patch size is much smaller. This patch modifies PuffinStream to cache only the Puff Buffers up to a maximum passed total memory size as a parameter to puffpatch. This acts as an LRU, the least recently used puff buffers are ejected when the cache is full. vm_tools: maitred: Implement proper shut down Implement proper VM shut down by having maitred first send a SIGTERM to all processes, wait up to 5 seconds for them to exit, and kill any stragglers with SIGKILL. maitred will then shut down the gRPC server before issuing a reboot() syscall. In practice, it takes ~1 second from the point that the server receives the request to the point that the reboot syscall is issued. In the worst case this can take an infinite amount of time if the gRPC server is unable to shut down. BUG=none TEST=manual. Start some long running processes and initiate a shutdown. See that the RPC is successful and the VM shuts down properly with no warning or error logs. Change-Id: I4df036b16035fa30561fc3210c622adb402d37e7 Signed-off-by: Chirantan Ekbote <chirantan@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/725520

tpm: provide means of shutting down comms layer while in reset Currently the Cr50 code resets TPM communications layer at a certain point during TPM reset process. It turns out that this is not sufficient - the comms layer keeps receiving and trying to invoke TPM layer, which does not mesh well with TPM reset. Let's provide two callbacks for each comms layer - to shut it down and to bring it back up. We shut down the comms when starting TPM reset and bring them back up when reset is completed. CHROMIUM: Revert "UPSTREAM: Bluetooth: btusb: driver to enable the usb-wakeup feature" This reverts commit 74f911a25030 ("UPSTREAM: Bluetooth: btusb: driver to enable the usb-wakeup feature"). The reason is that this causes any inband communication from the btusb device to cause the system to wake up. We know that the BT controller could be scanning when we decide to suspend and will send in the results once the scan is complete, thus failing the suspend entry. This is a temporary work around until the bug 67489211 is solved. We can put this back once the bluetoothd starts to listen to powerd for suspend requests and do the right thing. (Reverting this commit has the side effect that BLE mouse clicks do not wake up the system from suspend, but that is lesser price to pay than no going to suspend). Signed-off-by: Rajat Jain <rajatja@google.com> BUG=b:67489211, b:37256085 TEST=system can go to suspend even though BLE mouse is connected / scan is running Change-Id: I6ecefb750a3f5809ed5cb88662dac88fc453ad70 Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/750073 Commit-Ready: Rajat Jain <rajatja@chromium.org> Tested-by: Rajat Jain <rajatja@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Rajat Jain <rajatja@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Todd Broch <tbroch@chromium.org>

FROMLIST/BACKPORT: PM / s2idle: Clear the events_check_enabled flag Problem: This flag does not get cleared currently in the suspend or resume path in the following cases: * In case some driver's suspend routine returns an error. * Successful s2idle case * etc? Why is this a problem: What happens is that the next suspend attempt could fail even though the user did not enable the flag by writing to /sys/power/wakeup_count. This is 1 use case how the issue can be seen (but similar use case with driver suspend failure can be thought of): 1. Read /sys/power/wakeup_count 2. echo count > /sys/power/wakeup_count 3. echo freeze > /sys/power/state 4. Let the system suspend, and wakeup the system using some wake source that calls pm_wakeup_event() e.g. power button or something. 5. Note that the combined wakeup count would be incremented due to the pm_wakeup_event() in the resume path. 6. After resuming the events_check_enabled flag is still set. At this point if the user attempts to freeze again (without writing to /sys/power/wakeup_count), the suspend would fail even though there has been no wake event since the past resume. What this patch does: It moves the clearing of the flag to just before a resume is completed, so that it is always cleared for the corner cases mentioned above. Signed-off-by: Rajat Jain <rajatja@google.com> Acked-by: Pavel Machek <pavel@ucw.cz> (am from https://patchwork.kernel.org/patch/10035433/) BUG=b:65699528 TEST=Verify echo "freeze > /sys/power/state" works after a powerd_dbus_suspend Change-Id: Iec53b1b70adc7f8b326845f93d5a33f1beccd1c8 Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/746024 Commit-Ready: Rajat Jain <rajatja@chromium.org> Tested-by: Rajat Jain <rajatja@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Furquan Shaikh <furquan@chromium.org>

bluetooth: "Fix" sync of commands for adv & scan This is a very ugly hack, presented here in a very ugly way. The ugly way is basically how we deliver this only for eve and not affect other devices. The ugly hack is basically how we work aroung bluez's complete lack of synchronization. Let me explain. No, there is not time. Let me summarize: bluez has a boolean value for "are we scanning" which it updates inside the command-complete event handler. It also checks this in many places as a way to tell if the chip is or is not scanning. The issue is that some chips (like BCM's) let you disable something already disabled and do not raise a fuss. Other chips (like Intel's 7265) do raise a fuss if you try to disable scanning if it is already off. So why the issue? If the chip raises an error, bluez loses its marbles and gets out of sync with the chip. Basically it thinks the chip *IS* scanning while chip is not. There is no way out of this since any attempt to tell bluez to start scanning causes it to just reply with "already am" and any attempt to stop scanning sends the "scan disable" command to the chip and produces the same kind of error that got us into this mess. So how do we fix this? There isn't really a simple or elegant way. But the basic issue is that while a command to enable or disable scanning is in flight, any code in the stack will think scanning is still in the old state, while it may already be in the new state. This might cause more commands to be enqueued based on this errorneous information. To solve this we'd like to always have correct information. Sadly this is not easy. There is also a command queue, which at any point in time may have many command enqueued that affect scanning state. There are multiple ways to insert commands into it, and we do not want to instrument them all. So what do we do? First we add a second boolean bit for "scan state change command in flight". We set this when we *SEND TO THE CHIP* a command that affects scan state and clear it when a reply arrives. We also change all places that check the "are we scanning" state to properly consider this new variable as well. This will not solve the issue of many commands queued already. So it is still possible that while a "disable" was queued, another "disable" may be queued. To work around this we also track the current state in the lowest layer that actually sends commands to the chip and simply drop ones that would transition us to the same state that we're already in. The situation is actually weirder because there is a "restart" func in bluez all of whose callers seem to assume that it atomically toggles scanning off and back on if it is already on. No such atomicity exists in reality. Our hack covers up for this in most cases. Oh, and this same exact logic applies to "are we advertising" boolean and we treat it the same way. This really solves nothing, but it works around the issue well enough for our purposes. A proper fix would be a separate queue for state changes for "adv" and "scan" with proper suport for atomic "restart" requests. This queue would then submit actual commands to the chip's queue. since nobody else would do that, it would have no races. We have no time to produce such fixes, so for now you get to enjoy this dirty hack. This hack is based on initial work by josephsih@ who first figured out the proper place to filter all the low level commands as they are sent to the chip and the proper way to drop them. coral: Ensure battery report timer can be restarted Coral uses a 1 second delay to report battery being present to help avoid VSYS glitches than can affect H1. On Eve, it was not expected to remove and reconnect the battery while running. However, on Coral the battery connector allows this action to take place. Current if the battery is removed, when it's reconnected it can't report as present because the timer_started flag is not being reset. This CL checks for the case where the battery is not present after being present and uses that as a trigger to reset the battery_report_present_timer_started flag. BUG=b:66923031 BRANCH=coral TEST=While Coral unit has battery and ext AC connect, remove the battery connector. Verifed the console log showed that this condition was caught. Waited about 10 seconds, then reconnected battery and verified that it reports as present. [52.778818 Battery was present, but is now removed] [60.211048 battery will now report present] [60.217801 Battery FET: reg 0xe000 mask 0x4000 disc 0x0000] [60.711195 battery woke up] Change-Id: I41ae8c1b04a56697d20d3037b94189aff778fc4d Signed-off-by: Scott Collyer <scollyer@google.com> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/754025 Commit-Ready: Scott Collyer <scollyer@chromium.org> Tested-by: Scott Collyer <scollyer@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Duncan Laurie <dlaurie@google.com>
